title: Automated Code Review Using Large Language Models at Ericsson: An Experience Report
extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether large language models (LLMs) can help automate software code review in an industrial setting, reducing the burden on experienced developers while still producing useful review comments. The authors frame code review as an important but time-consuming quality assurance activity and investigate how LLMs might generate timely, relevant, and concise feedback on code changes made in Ericsson projects.

The intervention is a lightweight automated code review pipeline that combines static program analysis with open-source LLMs such as Llama 2, Code Llama, and Mixtral. Instead of sending only changed lines to the model, the system extracts the enclosing Java method for each code diff using Tree-Sitter and includes that context in prompts designed for succinct critical review. The tool was integrated into Ericsson workflows through Gerrit, a web interface, and a VS Code plugin. The study also compared outputs from different LLM sizes and variants and gathered feedback on prompt quality and practical usability.

The population consisted of experienced Ericsson software developers, primarily senior software engineers or above with at least three years of experience, working in an industry context rather than an educational one. Evaluation included surveys in which experts reviewed LLM-generated comments on real Ericsson code snippets, pairwise comparisons of reviews from different models, and a 15-day practical use period with the tool. Quantitative counts and qualitative comments were both reported.

The main conclusions are that the approach is promising but still imperfect. Experts provided a mix of positive, neutral, and negative feedback; larger Code Llama models appeared to perform best in the reported pairwise comparisons; and some developers felt the tool saved time and improved efficiency. However, reviews were sometimes irrelevant, factually incorrect, or overly explanatory. Overall, the paper presents an early-stage industrial experience report suggesting that context-aware prompting with lightweight open-source LLMs can support automated code review, while also highlighting the need for further refinement and broader evaluation.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an industry experience report with survey-based and small-scale exploratory evaluations, but no experimental or quasi-experimental design, no validated outcome measures, and no causal identification strategy. It provides some empirical evidence, yet credibility is limited by small samples, subjective measures, and preliminary analysis.
impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest potentially useful but inconsistent benefits for efficiency and review quality, with mixed self-reports and no reported effect sizes. Impact appears promising but unclear and modest at best based on the available evidence.

interventions.use_case: LLM-assisted automated code review for professional software developers, generating concise review comments on Java code changes using prompts plus static analysis to extract the enclosing method context.
Static program analysis used alongside the LLM to identify enclosing methods for changed lines and improve contextualization of generated code reviews.

finding.finding_summary: In a 15-day field survey with 9 expert developers, 4/9 reported the tool saved them time and 4/9 rated it effective or highly effective for improving coding efficiency, while 3/9 said it was not very effective. Usage was uneven (2 regular users, 5 occasional, 2 one-time users), and dissatisfaction centered on reviews that merely explained code, were factually incorrect, or focused on irrelevant areas. No standardized productivity effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Self-reported time savings, perceived coding efficiency, and frequency of tool use from developer survey

finding.finding_summary: Across a survey of 8 expert developers reviewing 10 LLM-generated code reviews, feedback included positive comments about meaningful suggestions, but also neutral and negative feedback indicating verbosity, incorrect details, irrelevant comments, and missed issues. The study suggests LLM reviews may support code-review reasoning and critical evaluation in some cases, but reliability is inconsistent and no quantitative learning gains were measured.
finding.measure: Expert judgments of review relevance, accuracy, usefulness, and qualitative comment categories on generated code reviews

finding.finding_summary: For software engineering task performance, the paper reports preliminary evidence that LLMs could detect injected bugs in 15 snippets (10 short, 5 medium) and generated reviews in roughly 5-6 seconds, but the main formal evaluation relied on expert opinion rather than validated performance outcomes. Pairwise comparisons across 36 evaluations suggested Code LLaMA 13B was preferred more often than other small models, though differences were based on vote counts rather than inferential statistics.
finding.measure: Bug-detection success in adversarial prompt tests, review latency, and pairwise expert preferences between LLM-generated reviews
finding.study_size: 36 pairwise comparisons by 9 experts; 15 adversarial snippets; 5 change IDs for unchanged-line behavior
